description:
Azimuth Zero

Semper ad septentrionem

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
In celestial mechanics and navigation, an azimuth of zero marks the true reference heading, the baseline orientation from which every bearing, vector, and trajectory is measured.

Drawing inspiration from this navigational datum, Azimuth Zero is tackling NASA's Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martial Map.
summary: Using satellite and topography data to plot a map and elevation of the Gale Crater and Curiosity science target locations to calculate the safest and most efficient route to an areas of scientific interest. The UI also displays wind speed, wind direction and ambient radiation to inform the feasibility of astronaut EVAs and surface excursions.
details:
Team Azimuth Zero's project: "Azimuth Atlas" aims to tackle the interplanetary survival guide: Martian map challenge by keeping astronauts on EVA's/Marswalks informed of ambient radiation and wind speed, as well as changes in elevation which may complicate their traversal.

We focused on the Gale Crater: the Curiosity Rover's landing zone and surrounding topography. The software allows astronauts to safely and efficiently navigate to NASA-defined points of interest by entering latitude and longitude coordinates, as well as a desired search radius.

The main program was coded in a Python with a tiny bit of CSS, in Microsoft Visual Basic. The presentation was made inside of Microsoft Powerpoint. Our team logo was made with vector graphics inside Affinity. Team coordination, task delegation and research pooling was handled through a shared Google Doc.

Our project was creative through its simple yet stylish UI, which followed a consistent colour scheme and design guide. The map in the centre provides users with the intriguing ability to switch between satellite and topographical view at will. The zoom in/out buttons allows for swift transitions between the calculated route view and the radius-point of interest view. Through danger thresholds, our system was also capable of alerting astronauts if there was a high risk of a dust storm or excessive radiation.

My team considered all factors of the lunar landscape, from the difficulty of traversing the landscape, to physical strain incurred by the astronauts and limited oxygen supplies.
